text.p: Profit-taking braked prices for coffee futures on Friday after their relentless rally while copper chalked up an 11-1/2 month high on the London Metal Exchange. But gold eased on German bullion reserve revaluation fears and a sell-off in silver. A volatile mix of low stocks, tight Latin American supply and worries that Brazil may have another frost has sent coffee futures on their longest sustained rally for two decades.

NEW YORK - COMEX copper ended slightly lower Friday, but gains from the week's rally remained largely intact as falling LME stocks, labor concerns and good demand underpinned prices, dealers said. COMEX's most-active July contract ended 0.20 cent weaker at 116.20 cents a lb, traded 116.40 to 115.40 cents. July finished the week up 4.60 cents. Spot May ended unchanged at 117.00 cents. Dealings Friday were sluggish as the market took a breather from Thursday's strong gains when prices settled at their highest in almost a year. Activity slowed in Friday afternoon LME trading, with the base metal complex's leading performers settling into a consolidatory mode, traders said. In copper, the early jump to a new 11-1/2 month high of $2,488 was not sustained, and by the end of the kerb three months was back at $2,466, up just $3 from Thursday's kerb. NEW YORK - New York precious metals ended sharply weaker Friday, the losses coming hard on the heels of Germany's plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves, rattling gold sentiment despite denials that not a single ounce of the central bank's hoard would be sold. COMEX June gold ended $3.50 lower at $344.90 an ounce, traded $347.90 to $344.30. Bullion was quoted mid-afternoon at $343.80/$344.30. London's closing fix was $344.50, down from $346.40 on Thursday. The downward spiral began with selling in silver, whose trading range had become narrow, leading to an inevitable breakout, dealers said. Gold then took the lead to push the precious metals complex lower as the platinum group metals, which had hitherto injected buoyancy into the complex, ran out of steam. COMEX July silver settled 16.5 cents lower at $4.693, traded $4.85 to $4.665. July NYMEX platinum settled $2.70 lower at $391.20, traded $393.50 to $389.50.

NEW YORK - NYMEX crude ended with sharp gains Friday after a technical breakout and a thinner Brent loading schedule sparked a sizzling rally. June crude ended 82 cents a barrel higher at $22.12 after surging as much as $1.10 to $22.40. Friday's technical breakout followed one Monday, giving prompt crude a gain of $1.69 a barrel for the week. Refined products were swept up in crude's gains, with June gasoline ending 1.83 cents a gallon higher at 65.87 cents. June heating oil finished 1.99 cents a gallon higher at 58.87 cents. In London, - IPE Brent crude oil futures soared in late trading on Friday, pushed up to two-month highs by institutional funds buying WTI futures in the United States and technical factors, brokers said. The front month July contract last traded at $20.35 a barrel, up 86 cents on yesterday's close.

CHICAGO - CBOT wheat futures closed higher on dry weather in portions of the Kansas wheat growing region and on spillover from Thursday's supportive USDA weekly export sales report, traders said. "There are some signs of a little better demand. The export sales (Thursday's USDA weekly) were better than some people thought," said Jack Scoville, Vice President for Price Futures Group. Wheat closed four cents higher to three lower, with May up four at $3.87 and new crop July 1/4 cent higher at $3.88-3/4. Technicians said the wheat market was oversold recently and was due for a correction. The nine day relative strength index (RSI) for the July reached a recent low of 31 percent at Wedneday's close and Friday closed at 34 percent. An RSI of 30 or less is indicative of an oversold market. Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 14,000 contracts, below the 17,147 traded Thursday.

NEW YORK - CSCE world sugar futures settled a thinly traded session lower as a dearth of fundamental news and upcoming industry events kept the market within a tight range, traders said. The July contract closed 0.04 cent weaker at 10.97 cents per lb, having ranged from 11.05 to 10.95. The outer contracts closed 0.01 lower to 0.04 higher. An estimated 8,668 lots changed hands against Thursday's official 7,248. Technically, a close below key 11.00 cents does not bode well for higher prices next week. But with many players in New York for the annual U.S. Cane Sugar Refiners' Association dinner on Wednesday, activity could remain rangebound and thin, industry sources said.
